topics: sequence length bucketing and kernel selection
transcript:
Meeting header: 2027-08-03 14:00 UTC | Duration: ~52m | Recording: enabled
Attendees: Jared (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Marco (Redwood Product), Alex (Arcadia CTO), Samir (Arcadia SRE), Maya (Arcadia ML), Liam (Arcadia PM)

[00:00] Jared: hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick agenda — triage the ttft oscillations we saw in the last pilot run, review streaming behavior, and agree next steps. anyone need to add?
[00:14] Alex: no, that sounds good. we just want to get to a stable first token median for chat flows.
[00:22] Priya: quick note — when i say kernel-a/kernel-c below those are the variants we used in the bench. kernel-c is the mixed quant path that reduces throughput variance but sometimes adds a small cold-start to kv cache.
[00:40] Samir: we've been seeing these spikes during our morning ingest window, microbursts — it looks like TTFT jumps from 80ms to 420ms for a subset of streaming sessions.
[00:58] Maya: right, and those sessions are mostly long seqlen customer support threads — average seqlen around 1.2k for those tails.
[01:12] Jared: ok that's helpful. priya, can you run through the perf summary you posted?
[01:23] Priya: sure — slide recap, apologies, i'm reading off the bench notes: stable load bench with 100rps steady, plus artificial microbursts of 500rps for 30s. With kernel-a we saw median ttft 78ms, p95 210ms; with kernel-c median 95ms, p95 180ms, but during microbursts kernel-c had a bimodal distribution — a cluster near 120ms and another around 380ms. transcription note: some words may be off in the bench CSV.
[02:05] Liam: when you say bimodal, is that per-request type or per-sequence length?
[02:11] Priya: a bit of both. the higher cluster correlates strongly with seqlen > 800 and streaming sessions where the prefix isn't cached. we've got a KV cache hit metric in the bench.
[02:27] Marco: one nuance — the serving runtime will pick a fast aten kernel for short seqlen but fall back to a more memory-conservative kernel when memory pressure is detected. that route switch can cause the oscillation.
[02:45] Alex: are we certain it's kernel selection and not load balancer queuing?
[02:51] Priya: we isolated LB influence by pinning requests to a single GPU node in the bench; oscillation persisted. so pointing to kernel pathway.
[03:05] Samir: interesting, our infra is pretty standard k8s autoscale, but we do see node-level GC/oom events around the same times, could be confounding.
[03:18] Maya: also note our quant profile is mixed — 4-bit on body, 8-bit for some attention layers. could that interplay be causing stutters?
[03:29] Priya: yes mixed quant can amplify path differences, at least in our experiments. the kernel that handles 4-bit ops has a slightly different dispatch latency.
[03:42] Jared: ok so plan A is run a hedged request experiment? explain what that would look like.
[03:49] Priya: hedged request means issue two parallel inference paths for the first token: one using kernel-a (fast short-seqlen path) and one using kernel-c (stable under pressure). whichever returns first, we use. cost is higher but can dramatically reduce TTFT tail. we also suggested a microburst hedging only for sessions flagged as long-seqlen candidates, so we limit cost.
[04:15] Alex: what's the expected cost impact? back-of-envelope?
[04:19] Marco: rough estimate — hedging for 10% of requests gives ~8-12% extra token cost but cuts p95 ttft by ~40-60% in our bench. numbers vary by model and seqlen distribution.
[04:35] Liam: could Redwood do adaptive hedging — only when queue depth exceeds X?
[04:39] Priya: yes that's possible — we can route by policy: seqlen estimate + runtime queue depth threshold. it's what we call smart routing.
[04:49] Samir: are there any caveats for streaming? our client uses a streaming websocket where handshake time matters. issuing two parallel paths — does that complicate the streaming handshake?
[04:59] Priya: it adds some complexity. for streaming we propose hedging at the first-token generation layer and only opening a single streaming session to the client; internally we race kernels, then continue streaming from whichever response finishes first. we keep the socket alive so no double-sends.
[05:18] Maya: sounds good. any perf delta on subsequent tokens?
[05:22] Priya: minimal if we reuse the selected KV cache. small overhead only at initial token.
[05:28] Alex: security question — hedging means more temporary state in memory, any risk for data residency or logs?
[05:34] Marco: no persistent storage; all inference state stays in memory. for Private deployments we can restrict memory regions and KMS integration remains unchanged.
[05:44] Liam: we had a question about SOC2 and audit logs for private — Jared?
[05:48] Jared: yes we'll follow up with the SOC2 pack and the audit log doc. i'll attach the KMS integration note too.

[06:05] [PRIYA screenshare perf CSV summary - audible clicking] 
[06:21] Priya: showing the seqlen bucket chart — majority 0-128, big tail 512-1024 and some outliers to 2k. the microburst-induced path switch lines up exactly with those >800 samples.
[06:40] Samir: can you bucket by prompt type? sometimes system prompts are huge and skew things.
[06:45] Priya: yes, we can after you give us the prompt tag mapping.
[06:49] Maya: we'll share tagging rules.

[07:01] Marco: also looked at streaming buffer size — if the runtime uses a 64KB buffer vs 256KB the handshake differences change. smaller buffer encourages earlier kernel fallback.
[07:16] Alex: is buffer size something we can toggle without redeploying?
[07:20] Priya: we can toggle at the config layer for Redwood Dedicated or Hosted with feature flag, yes. for Private on-prem you can also change it via runtime config.
[07:31] Liam: do we recommend a default?
[07:34] Marco: for Arcadia use-case we recommended 128KB as a balance. steady-state latency and memory tradeoff seemed best there.

[07:45] Jared: ok so immediate experiments: hedged kernel run, buffer size run, and a bench with pinned node and real trace. Priya will own hedged run.

[08:00] Priya: i'll also run a kernel midsize variant (kernel-b) with slightly different aten op ordering — may smooth the bimodality.
[08:08] Maya: curious if quantization tweak helps — do you have recommendations?
[08:12] Priya: short-term: tighten the attention-layer quant to 8-bit for long-seqlen models; long-term we can test mixed quant profiles per-layer per-kernel.
[08:22] Samir: also want to validate with our autoscaler off to rule out node churn.
[08:27] Priya: we'll run both with autoscale off and on.

[08:35] Alex: timeline? we'd like to show stable numbers in next week's review.
[08:39] Jared: sounds feasible. Priya will run hedging + buffer + kernel-b by Tuesday. Alex to upload trace by Friday. bench session Thu. i will send the calendar.

[08:53] Marco: quick procurement/price check — for dedicated burst capacity, Jared is that in the pricing sheet?
[08:59] Jared: yes i'll send updated pilot pricing; it includes burst pool with commit-minute buckets.
[09:07] Liam: do you support private deployment in our eu region? data residency is critical for some customers.
[09:11] Marco: yes Private supports EU region, can be VPC or on-prem. KMS/HSM integration is available.

[09:22] Maya: one last technical: we saw jitter on the kv cache warmup when two sessions race — could that cause a double-cache miss?
[09:29] Priya: possible, but we can sequence the KV state merge so only one wins and then warm the other. minor implementation but trivial for pilot.

[09:40] Alex: perfect, thanks all. can we recap next steps?
[09:44] Jared: recap: 1) Priya hedged kernel + kernel-b + buffer runs and upload CSVs by 2027-08-10; 2) Arcadia uploads 24h trace + prompt tags by 2027-08-06; 3) bench session Thu 2027-08-11 16:00 UTC with infra leads; 4) Jared sends pricing and SOC2/KMS docs by 2027-08-05.
[10:08] Samir: noted.
[10:12] Jared: any blockers?
[10:14] Alex: none, thanks.
[10:17] Jared: great, wrap up. thanks everyone.

End of transcription.
